title: [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois..., pages 650 bis à 787, dont table des matières] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 769–771 of the continuation of La Longue Marche): Grothendieck builds a homotopy-free theory of the fundamental group for 'germes d'espaces' (the transcription's 'genres' is almost certainly 'germes'). A germ is a pair (S, 𝔏): a space S together with a filter 𝔏 of subsets of S. A covering of the germ is a covering of some member S_i ∈ 𝔏, and two such coverings are identified if they agree on a smaller member of the filter, so Rev(S, 𝔏) is a 2-colimit of the categories Rev(S_i). Topological spaces sit fully faithfully inside germs via X ↦ (X, trivial filter {X}).

The point of the construction is base points. Instead of a point, a base point is a 1-connected germ 𝔖 with a morphism 𝔖 → 𝔛; '1-connected' means Rev(𝔖) ≃ (Ens). Pulling coverings back along 𝔖 → 𝔛 gives a fibre functor Rev(𝔛) → Rev(𝔖) ≃ Ens (formula 49). This defines π₁(𝔛, 𝔖) (formula 50). If 𝔛 is connected and Rev(𝔛) is galoisienne, this page's formula (51) gives Rev(𝔛) ≃ Ens(π), the category of π-sets.

This page then makes three points.
(i) π₁(𝔛, 𝔖) is functorial in the arrow 𝔖 → 𝔛, viewed in the category of germs with 1-connected source.
(ii) For a space X and a subset Y ⊂ X, two germs are defined:
- the germ of X around Y is (X, filter of neighbourhoods of Y);
- the residual germ is the induced germ on X∖Y, i.e. the deleted-neighbourhood germ. It is empty iff Y is open.
The main case is Y = {x}. The germ at x is trivially 1-connected: any covering of a neighbourhood is trivial on a smaller neighbourhood. The residual germ in general is not.
(iii) The last lines are only partly legible. They apparently state a converse: every germ (S, 𝔏) can be realised as the residual germ of the space S ∪ {ω} at a suitable point ω. One topologises S ∪ {ω} so that the neighbourhoods of ω are {ω} ∪ S_i with S_i ∈ 𝔏.

Purpose (next page): take x a point of a surface, with a neighbourhood ≅ ℝ². The residual germ D*_x is a punctured-disc germ with π₁ ≅ ℤ, a local inertia group. Grothendieck wants to choose a 'universal covering' of it and digresses on universal coverings of abstract germs. In other words he is setting up base points at a puncture: a 1-connected germ such as a sector, mapping into the punctured-disc germ. This is the topological skeleton of 'tangential base points' at cusps/punctures, needed for the Galois action on fundamental groupoids of curves and moduli (Teichmüller tower).
errors: Formula (51) as an equivalence with Ens(π) for a discrete group needs Rev(𝔛) to be (multi)galoisienne. For an arbitrary germ the colimit of covering categories may behave poorly (e.g. not locally connected), so this assumption carries real content; Grothendieck states it as a hypothesis, so this is not an error.
Minor: the parenthetical says the residual germ is empty iff Y is open. This is right in the filter sense (the induced filter on X∖Y contains ∅). The page is consistent.

missed.claim: Grothendieck formalizes base points as arbitrary 1-connected germs mapping into a (residual) germ of a space. Applied to punctured-disc germs at points of surfaces, this is a purely topological framework for tangential base points at punctures. It predates or is independent of Deligne's 1989 formalization, and is more general (any 1-connected germ, functorial in the arrow).
missed.quote: Le groupe π₁(𝔛, 𝔖) dépend fonctoriellement des triples (𝔖, 𝔛, 𝔖→𝔛) i.e. de la flèche 𝔖→𝔛 dans la catégorie des germes d'espaces, où la source 𝔖 est 1-connexe.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It documents Grothendieck's own route to tangential base points and inertia at cusps in the Teichmüller-tower program. That route is relevant to the history and to anabelian/GT literature, where the construction is usually credited to Deligne and Ihara.

deep.surprise_reason: A clean but mostly foundational setup: germs, fibre functors from 1-connected germs, residual germs at points. Its interest is historical. It shows Grothendieck developing a general 'germ base point' formalism behind tangential base points, which in the literature is credited to Deligne (1989). No deep new theorem appears.
transcription_corrections: 'genres d'espaces' (previous page) is very likely 'germes d'espaces', matching this page.
Line after 'partie de X': probably 'on appelle germe de X autour de Y le germe d'espace (X, 𝔏)'.
'(il est vide ssi Y est ...ert)' should be '(il est vide ssi Y est ouvert)'.
'(NB le germe de X en x est trivialement 1-connexe, ...germe résiduel)' is likely '..., mais pas en général le germe résiduel)'.

Final lines are likely: 'Inversement, tous les germes d'espaces (S, 𝔏) peuvent s'interpréter comme germe résiduel d'un espace X = S∪{ω} en un pt ω convenable…'; 'pointés singuliers' looks like a misreading.
On the next page, 'groupe résiduel' and 'groupe d'inertie[?]' are likely 'germe résiduel' and 'germe d'espace'.
